engineering.hero_tagline: From AR Ventus 2.27 to AR Nimbus 4.51 — the real specs, the CAD process, the physics, and the lessons learned building each car.

evolution.heading: Two Cars, One Relentless Redesign
evolution.body:
Every Aerostorm car carries a version number that tracks its design iteration count — 2.27, for example, marks the 27th iteration of our second concept line. It's a small detail, but an honest one: nothing on the car arrived on the first try.

AR Nimbus 4.51 didn't start on a clean sheet — it's a direct rebuild of what we learned racing AR Ventus 2.27 at regionals.

cards.label: Regional Qualifier
cards.title: AR Ventus 2.27
items: A gap between the wheel and sidepod edge increased friction and hurt aerodynamics.
Ran a plain axle-hole wheel system with no bearings, costing performance.

cards.label: Nationals · Current
cards.title: AR Nimbus 4.51
items: Sidepod lengthened within regs while managing weight — airflow is more linear and the part is actually manufacturable on the CNC.
Replaced the axle-hole system with Axle → Bearing Holder → Wheel, using F1 Bearing's Hybrid Ceramic Bearings.

aerodynamics.heading: Designed to Cut Through the Air

rows.text: minimizes the stagnation zone, while the body's top surface transitions gradually into the cockpit hump with no sharp corners — keeping airflow attached longer and avoiding early boundary-layer separation and turbulent wake.
— a deliberately moderate angle, enough for downforce and grip without excessive drag on a straight track.
, a browser-based CFD/CAA tool, to visualize airflow — this is what caught the Ventus sidepod flaw before Nimbus was built.

cad.heading: From Sketch to Solid

cards.title: Main Body
cards.text: Modeled with Fusion's loft tool to build the continuous body surface.

cards.title: Sidepod & Wings
cards.text: Built with sketch, extrude, and fillet operations.

cards.title: Wheel & Axle
cards.text: Assembled with Fusion's joint tool — axles get revolute motion, wheels get circular motion.

materials: Main car body — CNC-machined Polyurethane foam
Halo, helmet, front wing, rear wing, bearings, bearing holders, wheels — PLA-CF

cards.text: Used to compare material acceleration — PLA-CF's lower mass versus alternatives gave better acceleration.
The drag equation, used to reason about reducing frontal area and drag.
Early-stage balloon-rocket experiments estimated achievable velocity, targeting roughly an 80% drag reduction from initial concepts.

manufacturing.heading: Built By Hand, Machined With Precision

rows.text: — test iterations 3D-printed on a Bambu Lab A1, reusing old and near-empty filament spools and parts from prior prototypes.
— CNC-machined by Stemplify, our manufacturing partner.
— axle holes drilled at home, front wing joints sawed for proper fit, and loose-fitting pieces hand-assembled with super glue.
— sprayed by sponsor House of Polish.

cards.title: Bearing Fix, On the Fly
cards.text: Testing at the Official STEM Racing India track surfaced a bearing-rotation issue that was loosening the wheel. Fixed by adding a thin layer of paint over the axle protrusion that inserts into the bearing, tightening the joint.

cards.title: Simulated vs. Real Weight
cards.text: Fusion's simulated weight estimates were well off from the real build: the bearing assembly alone came in at ~34g, heavier than expected, and the real main body weighed 68g against Fusion's simulated 36g — roughly double. A lesson learned for the next iteration, not a failure.
